# Building the Commercial System at 20, 50 and 200 People

Source: https://lowob.com/research/building-the-commercial-system-at-every-size/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-08 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Thirty parts describe a full commercial system. No firm should build all of it at once. This capstone maps each part to three sizes, using lowob's scale ladder: at 20 people the job is to write the founder's system down, at 50 to make words mean the same thing across teams, and at 200 to let reasoning travel without its author. For each size it sets out what to own, what to rent and what to leave until the next rung.

The commercial system is the same set of decisions at every size: who to sell to, how to reach them, what to charge, what to forecast and how to learn from the result. What changes is the problem it has to solve. At around 20 people, the system lives in the founders' heads and the job is to write it down. At around 50, the same words start to mean different things in different teams, and the job is shared definitions with owners. At around 200, managers make most decisions, and the job is reasoning that travels without its author. Build for the next size, not two sizes up.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

Thirty parts ago we set out to describe the commercial system as a whole, from positioning to pricing experiments. Read as a list, it looks like a 500-person firm's operating manual.

No firm should build it all at once. A 20-person firm with a revenue operations team, a partner programme and a quarterly business review for every account is not mature. It is spending scarce attention on problems it does not yet have, and missing the one it does.

## The rule: build for the next size

**lowob**'s [*The scale ladder*](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/) describes the problems a company meets as it grows: false shared memory at two people, the first stranger at about ten, meaning at about fifty, delegation at about two hundred, and governance at about a thousand. The rungs are approximate. A regulated fintech may meet governance at 80 people; a research-heavy firm may stay at the meaning problem for years. The diagnosis is by problem, not headcount.

Its central rule is the one this capstone applies: build the layer the next stage will break, not the one the stage after that. [*Buy context, own judgment*](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/) adds the second rule: rent the context layer as it matures, and own the record of how you decide.

Each part of the commercial system has a minimum version and a full version. The question at each size is which one, and the honest answer is usually smaller than the plan.

There is outside evidence that the pressures grow with size. The US Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey found AI use rising over the six months to May 2026 among firms with 20 or more employees, reaching 32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees and 37% of those with 250 or more, while use among firms under 20 did not change significantly. Bessemer Venture Partners' analysis of cloud companies found general and administrative spending falling from about 70% of revenue at $1 million to $10 million of annual recurring revenue to about 20% beyond $50 million, while sales and marketing stayed at around half of revenue or more. The commercial system is the part of the firm that stays expensive as it grows, which is why it repays being built at the right size. Bain's research on what it calls the founder's mentality adds the organisational side. Its Founder's Mentality score fell from 72.3 out of 100 among companies with revenues of $500 million or less to 56.1 among those of $5 billion or more. In the same work, 85% of executives surveyed said internal obstacles, not external ones, kept their companies from growing profitably. Those are much larger firms than this series addresses, but the direction is the same: growth breaks the way decisions are made before it breaks the market.

## At around 20 people: write the founder's system down

At 20 people the commercial system usually works, because the founder runs it. The founder knows which customers fit, what the last discount was and why the big deal stalled. The problem the scale ladder names for this stage is the first stranger: people join who were not there for the history, and they cannot ask the founder everything. Our piece [*Ten people: the first stranger*](https://lowob.com/research/ten-people-the-first-stranger/) covers it in detail.

The job is therefore to write down a small number of things, in a form a newcomer can use.

**A one-page ICP** (Part 3, and [*How to write an ICP*](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/)). Which customers to pursue and which to decline, with reasons.

**One pipeline with written stage definitions** ([*What are pipeline stage definitions?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/)). Five or six stages, each with an exit criterion a stranger could apply.

**A weekly commercial meeting** (Part 6). Thirty minutes on pipeline, decisions due and last week's outcomes.

**A loss reason that includes no decision** ([*What is a closed-lost reason?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/)). One field, filled honestly.

**A founders' ledger of commercial calls.** Pricing exceptions, pursue-or-pass choices and big discounts, each with a reason. [*Two people: the founders' ledger*](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/) describes the habit.

**A simple discount rule.** A standard limit and one person who approves anything beyond it (Part 21).

What to leave: a revenue operations team, a formal partner programme, a key account programme and any tool that needs an administrator. The distribution parts (14 to 19) describe choices a 20-person firm should make once, deliberately, rather than build programmes around.

## At around 50 people: make the words mean the same thing

At 50 people there are teams, and each team has started to use the commercial vocabulary in its own way. Marketing's qualified lead is not sales' qualified opportunity. "Committed" means one thing in the forecast call and another in the board pack. Our piece [*Fifty people: when words start to mean different things*](https://lowob.com/research/fifty-people-when-words-start-to-mean-different-things/) describes the pattern.

The job at this size is shared meaning, with owners.

**Definitions with owners.** Stage definitions, forecast categories, the ICP and the main KPIs (Part 7), each with a named owner and a change log.

**Decision rights.** Who can approve a discount, a non-standard term, a partner deal or a change to a forecast category. Written down, so nobody negotiates authority deal by deal.

**One home for the record.** Commercial decisions recorded in one place with the same fields: decision, reason, owner, status, expected outcome with a check date, and the outcome written back ([*The commercial decisions worth recording*](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)).

**A monthly rhythm** on top of the weekly one: pipeline quality, forecast against outcome, and the decisions due for a check.

**A first capacity model** (Part 26). The Bridge Group's 2026 study put average AE ramp at 6.2 months; at 50 people, a hiring plan that ignores ramp will miss the year.

**A handover pack template** (Part 27) and **a few win-loss interviews a month** (Part 25), run by someone outside the deal team.

What to leave: a full deal desk, a dedicated revenue operations function, a formal partner tiering scheme and an ontology of commercial concepts. The glossary with owners is enough.

## At around 200 people: let reasoning travel without its author

At 200 people, managers make most commercial decisions, and the founder no longer sees them. The problem the scale ladder names is delegation: the reasons behind decisions must reach people who were not in the room. Our piece [*Two hundred people: reasoning that travels without its author*](https://lowob.com/research/two-hundred-people-reasoning-that-travels-without-its-author/) sets out what breaks.

The job is to turn the habits of the 50-person firm into routines that do not depend on particular people.

**Decision classes and templates.** The ten or so commercial decisions that recur, each with a template that asks for the same fields.

**A deal desk** for pricing exceptions, non-standard terms and complex quotes, with approval records the handover can link to.

**A revenue operations function.** Gartner predicted in 2021 that by 2025, 75% of the highest-growth companies would deploy a revenue operations model, to break down silos between sales, marketing and customer success. Forrester's 2024 definition stresses that revenue operations should not become another silo, and can sit within sales or marketing. At 200 people it is usually a small team that owns definitions, data and the planning cycle ([*What is revenue operations?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-operations/)).

**A standing win-loss programme**, a **top-twenty account routine** (Part 28), a **quarterly planning cycle** with capacity built from your own ramp and attainment history, and **pricing experiments** run with a decision rule (Part 29).

**First calibration.** Forecasts and expected outcomes recorded with a probability and checked against results ([*Calibration is the honest learning signal*](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/)).

What to leave: a platform team, a single enterprise-wide data model, and the governance apparatus of a 1,000-person firm, unless regulation brings it forward.

> The commercial system is the same set of decisions at every size. What changes is who makes them, and whether the reasons survive.

## The full map

The table maps each part of the series to the three sizes. "Minimum" means the smallest version that does the job; "full" means the version described in the part itself.

| Part of the system | Around 20 people | Around 50 people | Around 200 people |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Positioning and segments (Parts 2, 3, 5) | One-page ICP and positioning | ICP with an owner; one market map | Segment plans with evidence; market map used in account selection |
| Pricing architecture (Part 4) | One price list, one discount limit | Packages and decision rights | Pricing experiments with a decision rule (Part 29) |
| Operating rhythm (Part 6) | Weekly meeting | Weekly plus monthly | Weekly, monthly and quarterly |
| KPIs (Part 7) | Five numbers the founder trusts | Defined KPIs with owners | Board-grade KPIs with a definition log |
| Demand and content (Parts 8 to 13) | Founder-led, a few channels | First team-led programme with a cost per opportunity | Full demand economics and brand measures |
| Distribution (Parts 14 to 19) | One deliberate partner or channel choice | First partner programme with rules of engagement | Channel design and conflict rules |
| Qualification and proposals (Parts 20, 22) | A short qualification checklist | One framework, one proposal template | Proposal standards and review |
| Discount governance (Part 21) | One limit, one approver | Decision rights by size | Deal desk with recorded exceptions |
| Forecasting and capacity (Parts 23, 26) | Founder's forecast with a written reason | Forecast categories and a first capacity model | Calibrated forecast; capacity from own history |
| Renewals and handover (Parts 24, 27) | Founder or seller handles both | Handover pack template; renewal dates tracked | Joint handover on large deals; renewal and expansion plays |
| Win-loss and account planning (Parts 25, 28) | Loss reason with no decision | A few interviews a month; plans for the top eight to ten | Standing programme; monthly top-twenty review |

## Own, rent, not yet

The second rule, rent context and own judgment, gives each size a short list. It is consistent with the size guide in [*Buy context, own judgment*](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/), applied to the commercial line.

| Size | Rent | Own | Not yet |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Around 20 | A CRM used as it comes; an assistant; transcription | ICP, stage definitions, founders' ledger of commercial calls | Revenue operations team, wiki, integrations beyond the CRM |
| Around 50 | Meeting and writing tools that export; enrichment | Glossary with owners, decision rights, one home for the record | Ontology, deal desk software, partner portal |
| Around 200 | Workflow tools that can hold a precedent; forecasting and conversation tools | Decision classes, templates, handover packs, first calibration | Platform team, single enterprise data model |

Before renting anything that touches decisions, apply the export test from that piece: can the tool export every decision record with its history, will the records survive a change of vendor, and does the firm control retention? If not, keep the record elsewhere and let the tool read from it.

## How to tell you have moved up a size

Headcount is a rough guide. These symptoms are better ones.

| Symptom | What it means | What to build next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New sellers ask the founder the same questions | The first-stranger problem has arrived | Written ICP, stage definitions, ledger |
| Marketing and sales disagree about lead counts | Meaning has diverged | Definitions with owners |
| Discounts are negotiated internally deal by deal | Decision rights are missing | Written approval limits |
| The forecast misses in the same direction each quarter | Capacity and forecast are not reconciled | Capacity model; calibration |
| A senior seller leaves and an account wobbles | Reasoning lives in one person | Account plans and handover packs |
| Managers make calls the leadership cannot reconstruct | Delegation has arrived | Decision classes and templates |

The scale ladder suggests revisiting the diagnosis each time headcount roughly doubles. For the commercial system, the annual plan is the natural moment.

Illustrative example: a 60-person firm resisting the 200-person build

Decision
:   Defer a dedicated revenue operations team and deal desk software for a year; instead, give the head of sales operations ownership of definitions and write decision rights for discounts.

Reason and owner
:   The symptoms present were divergent definitions and negotiated discounts, both 50-person problems. Delegation symptoms were not yet visible. Owned by the chief executive, agreed with the revenue lead.

What changed
:   A glossary with owners, a discount approval table and one home for commercial decisions. The diagnosis is revisited at the next annual plan.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Build for the next size.** The commercial system should solve the problem you are about to meet, not one two rungs away.
- **At 20, write it down.** ICP, stage definitions, a weekly rhythm and a ledger of commercial calls.
- **At 50, agree the words.** Definitions with owners, decision rights and one home for the record.
- **At 200, let reasoning travel.** Decision classes, a deal desk, revenue operations and calibration.

Gateway card

### Before your next annual commercial plan

- The firm's current size problem named: first stranger, meaning or delegation
- The symptoms table checked against the last two quarters
- The map row for each part of the system reviewed, with the current version noted
- One thing to build for the next size, and one thing deliberately deferred
- Every tool touching decisions checked against the export test
- The plan recorded with its reasons, owner and check date
